questions.question: A custom middleware neither sends a response nor calls `next()`. What happens?
options: Express automatically calls `next()` after the function returns
Express responds with 500 Internal Server Error
The request hangs until the client or server times out
questions.explanation: Middleware must either end the request-response cycle or call `next()`. If it does neither, nothing else runs and the client waits until a timeout.

questions.question: Where should an `app.use(requireAuth)` call go so that `/public` is open but `/portfolio` is protected?
options: After `/public` is registered and before `/portfolio` is registered
At the very end of the file, after all routes
Anywhere; Express sorts middleware by path specificity
questions.explanation: Middleware runs in registration order. Routes registered before `app.use(requireAuth)` are not affected by it; routes registered after it are.

questions.question: What does calling `next(err)` with an Error object do?
options: Skips the remaining normal middleware and routes and runs error-handling middleware
Logs the error and continues to the next middleware normally
Ends the response with the error message as plain text immediately
questions.explanation: Passing any value other than "route" or "router" to `next()` signals an error, so Express jumps to middleware with the four-argument `(err, req, res, next)` signature.

questions.question: Why does a request-timing middleware listen for `res.on("finish")` instead of logging right before calling `next()`?
options: Because `next()` is asynchronous and never returns
Because `finish` is the only event that has access to `req`
Because Express forbids logging inside middleware
Because the final status code and total duration are only known after the response has been sent
questions.explanation: The middleware runs before the handler, so at that point the status code and elapsed time are unknown. The `finish` event fires once the response is sent, giving accurate values.
